qs.q: Which infectious agent causes Lymphogranuloma venereum, characterized by a small primary ulcer accompanied by painful inguinal lymphadenopathy?
qs.e: Lymphogranuloma venereum is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-L3, featuring a small ulcer and painful inguinal buboes. Treponema pallidum causes syphilis, which typically presents with a painless ulcer.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is a sexually transmitted infection caused by Chlamydia trachomatis L1‑L3. It begins with a brief genital ulcer and progresses to painful inguinal/femoral lymphadenopathy.

sections.p: LGV is an STI characterised by a transient genital ulcer followed by tender, often unilateral, inguinal or femoral lymph node enlargement. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern and confirmation by nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) from ulcer or lymph node tissue.
b: Typical ‘groove sign’ – a depression between enlarged inguinal nodes.
NAAT positive for C. trachomatis L1‑L3 confirms the diagnosis.

sections.p: LGV is staged into three clinical phases: primary (ulcer), secondary (buboes), and tertiary (proctocolitis or genital elephantiasis). Staging guides treatment duration and need for surgical drainage.
b: Stage I – painless ulcer, often unnoticed.
Stage II – painful buboes, may coalesce.
Stage III – chronic fibrosis, strictures, fistulae.

sections.p: LGV is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, and L3, transmitted through unprotected sexual contact, especially among men who have sex with men (MSM). Co‑infection with HIV is common and worsens outcomes.
b: C. trachomatis L1‑L3 (primary cause).
Concurrent HIV infection increases severity.
Other STIs (syphilis, gonorrhoea) may coexist.

sections.p: After a brief, often painless ulcer, patients develop tender inguinal/femoral lymphadenopathy that may become fluctuant. Systemic symptoms (fever, malaise) are common in the secondary phase.
b: Small ulcer <5 mm, heals in days.
Painful ‘bubo’ with overlying erythema.
Groove sign when nodes above and below inguinal ligament enlarge.

sections.p: Targeted testing confirms the pathogen and assesses complications. When NAAT is unavailable, serology or dark‑field microscopy of ulcer exudate may be used, acknowledging lower sensitivity.

t.a: NAAT from ulcer or lymph node aspirate
t.b: Does the patient have C. trachomatis L1‑L3? Positive result confirms LGV; negative with high suspicion → repeat or use alternative specimen.
Is there an abscess requiring drainage? Shows fluid collection; if unavailable, clinical exam guides need for incision and drainage.
Is the patient co‑infected? Positive result prompts closer monitoring and antiretroviral linkage.

sections.p: Uncontrolled infection can lead to chronic lymphatic obstruction, genital elephantiasis, rectal strictures, or systemic sepsis. Rapidly enlarging, fluctuant nodes demand urgent drainage.
b: Fever >38.5 °C with expanding buboes.
Signs of systemic infection (tachycardia, hypotension).
Development of fistulae or severe fibrosis.
Doxycycline – kills intracellular C. trachomatis; long course prevents relapse.
Avoid macrolides alone – lower cure rates for LGV.
Incision and drainage for fluctuant buboes to prevent sepsis.

sections.p: Re‑evaluate after 2 weeks to ensure lesion resolution. Counsel on condom use, partner notification, and HIV testing. Treat all sexual contacts empirically.
b: Clinical review at 2 weeks; repeat NAAT if symptoms persist.
Notify and treat recent partners within 60 days.
Educate on safe sex to prevent reinfection.

sections.p: Several conditions mimic LGV’s lymphadenopathy or ulcerative phase.
b: Syphilis primary chancre – painless ulcer but lacks painful buboes.
Chancroid – painful ulcer with tender nodes, caused by Haemophilus ducreyi.
Tuberculous lymphadenitis – chronic, non‑fluctuant nodes, often without ulcer.

sections.p: Certain tests may give false‑negative or ambiguous findings, leading to delayed treatment.
b: NAAT may be negative if taken after ulcer has healed; repeat from lymph node tissue.
Serology for Chlamydia is not reliable for LGV; a negative result does not rule it out.

whenToSeekHelp: High fever with rapidly enlarging inguinal buboes
Signs of sepsis (low blood pressure, rapid heart rate)
Development of fistulae or severe genital swelling

faq.q: Why is doxycycline preferred over azithromycin for LGV?
faq.a: Doxycycline penetrates intracellularly and has proven efficacy in a 21‑day course, whereas azithromycin’s single‑dose regimens are less reliable for LGV.

faq.q: Can LGV be transmitted without a visible ulcer?
faq.a: Yes; the primary ulcer is often unnoticed, so transmission can occur during the asymptomatic phase.

faq.q: Is HIV testing mandatory in LGV patients?
faq.a: While not mandatory, HIV co‑infection is common and influences management, so testing is strongly recommended.

exam: Describe the three clinical stages of LGV and their key features.
Explain why doxycycline is the drug of choice for LGV and list an alternative regimen.
Identify two red‑flag complications of LGV that require urgent intervention.
